issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when the existing record is insufficient to determine fair compensation and the proposed evidence bears directly on that determination.
material_facts: The appeal concerned a claim for enhanced compensation for acquired land.
The only evidence before the Reference Court and High Court was a sale deed that had been rejected, leaving no other material to determine fair market value.
The claimant sought to introduce sale deeds and certified copies of awards in other land acquisition cases, which could bear directly on the acquired land’s fair market value.
The High Court rejected the application without addressing whether the additional evidence was needed to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s rejection of the application was set aside, and the application to adduce the additional evidence was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC, additional evidence is not admitted as of right. The controlling consideration is whether the appellate court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence, or whether the evidence is required for another substantial cause. Its relevance to the issue and whether the applicant had an earlier opportunity to produce it are not, by themselves, decisive. The Court relied on A. Andisamy Chettiar v. A. Subburaj, (2015) 17 SCC 713.

predicates.compensation_appeal: A party appeals a decision determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.valuation_record_insufficient: The evidence in the existing record is insufficient to determine the fair value of the acquired land.
predicates.proposed_evidence_directly_bears_on_valu: The party seeks to introduce evidence that bears directly on determining the fair value of the acquired land.
predicates.appellate_court_cannot_pronounce_judgmen: The appellate court cannot adequately pronounce judgment on the existing record without the proposed evidence.

issues.definition: When a compensation appeal has an insufficient valuation record and the appellate court cannot pronounce judgment without proposed evidence that directly bears on valuation, the appellate court allows that additional evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Documents admitted as additional evidence must be proved before they can be considered, and the matter may be remanded to allow that proof and a fresh decision.
material_facts: The Court allowed the claimant to bring the proposed sale deeds and certified copies of awards on record as additional evidence.
The documents had not yet been proved as to their existence, authenticity, genuineness, or contents.
The Reference Court needed to receive and assess the proof before determining compensation afresh.
issues.conclusion: Admission of the documents did not make them automatically exhibitable or establish their contents. The claimant had to prove them in accordance with law before they could be considered, and the matter was remanded to the Reference Court for that purpose and a fresh decision.
issues.legal_principle: Allowing an application under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC does not itself establish additional documents or permit them to be taken into consideration without proof. The applicant must prove their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents in accordance with law. The Court relied on Uttaradi Mutt v. Raghavendra Swamy Mutt, (2018) 10 SCC 484.

predicates.civil_appeal_with_additional_documents_a: A court in a civil appeal admits documents as additional evidence.
predicates.documents_not_yet_proved: The admitted documents have not yet been proved as to their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents.

issues.definition: When documents are admitted as additional evidence in a civil appeal but have not yet been proved, they must be proved before they can be considered.
